Main.sentence: A nuclear weapon [a] is an ___E:explosive device U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_device)___ that derives its destructive force from ___E:nuclear reactions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reaction)___ , either ___E:nuclear fission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission)___ (fission or atomic bomb) or a combination of fission and ___E:nuclear fusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion)___ reactions ( ___E:thermonuclear weapon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermonuclear_weapon)___ [b] ), producing a ___E:nuclear explosion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_explosion)___ .
Both bomb types release large quantities of ___E:energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy)___ from relatively small amounts of ___E:matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matter)___ .

Nuclear weapons have had ___E:yields U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_yield)___ between 10 tons (the ___E:W54 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W54)___ ) and 50 megatons for the ___E:Tsar Bomba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba)___ (see ___E:TNT equivalent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_equivalent)___ ).
Yields in the low kilotons can devastate cities.
A thermonuclear weapon weighing as little as 600 pounds (270 kg) can release energy equal to more than 1.2 megatons of TNT (5.0 ___E:PJ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petajoule)___ ).

Apart from the blast, ___E:effects of nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_nuclear_weapons)___ include extreme ___E:heat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_radiation)___ and ___E:ionizing radiation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionizing_radiation)___ , ___E:firestorms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestorm)___ , radioactive ___E:nuclear fallout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fallout)___ , an ___E:electromagnetic pulse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_electromagnetic_pulse)___ , and a ___E:radar blackout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_blackout)___ .

The first nuclear weapons were developed by the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_the_United_States)___ in collaboration with the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ and ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ during ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ in the ___E:Manhattan Project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project)___ .

Production requires a large scientific and industrial complex, primarily for the production of ___E:fissile material U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile_material)___ , either from ___E:nuclear reactors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor)___ with ___E:reprocessing plants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reprocessing)___ or from ___E:uranium enrichment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_uranium)___ facilities.

Nuclear weapons have been used twice in ___E:war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War)___ , in the 1945 ___E:atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki)___ that killed between 150,000 and 246,000 people. ___E:Nuclear deterrence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterrence_theory)___ , including ___E:mutually assured destruction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction)___ , aims to prevent ___E:nuclear warfare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warfare)___ via the threat of unacceptable damage and the danger of escalation to ___E:nuclear holocaust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_holocaust)___ .

A ___E:nuclear arms race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_arms_race)___ for weapons and their delivery systems was a defining component of the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ .

___E:Strategic nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_nuclear_weapon)___ are targeted against civilian, industrial, and military infrastructure, while ___E:tactical nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_nuclear_weapons)___ are intended for battlefield use. Strategic weapons led to the development of dedicated ___E:intercontinental ballistic missiles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile)___ , ___E:submarine-launched ballistic missile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine-launched_ballistic_missile)___ , and nuclear ___E:strategic bombers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bomber)___ , collectively known as the ___E:nuclear triad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_triad)___ .

Tactical weapons options have included shorter-range ground-, air-, and sea-launched missiles, ___E:nuclear artillery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_artillery)___ , ___E:atomic demolition munitions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_demolition_munition)___ , ___E:nuclear torpedos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_torpedo)___ , and ___E:nuclear depth charges U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_depth_charge)___ , but they have become less salient since the end of the Cold War.

As of 2025 [update] , there are nine countries on the ___E:list of states with nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons)___ , and six more agree to ___E:nuclear sharing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing)___ .

Nuclear weapons are ___E:weapons of mass destruction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , and their control is a focus of ___E:international security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_security)___ through measures to prevent ___E:nuclear proliferation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_proliferation)___ , ___E:arms control U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control)___ , or ___E:nuclear disarmament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament)___ .
The total from all stockpiles peaked at over 64,000 weapons in 1986,  and is around 9,600 today.

Key international agreements and organizations include the ___E:Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ , the ___E:Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty)___ and ___E:Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty_Organization)___ , the ___E:International Atomic Energy Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency)___ , the ___E:Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ , and ___E:nuclear-weapon-free zones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon-free_zone)___ .

Nuclear weapons have only twice been used in warfare, both times by the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ against ___E:Japan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan)___ at the end of ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

On August 6, 1945, the ___E:United States Army Air Forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces)___ (USAAF) detonated a ___E:uranium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium)___ gun-type ___E:fission bomb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_bomb)___ nicknamed " ___E:Little Boy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Boy)___ " over the Japanese city of ___E:Hiroshima U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima)___ ; three days later, on August 9, the USAAF  detonated a ___E:plutonium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium)___ implosion-type fission bomb nicknamed " ___E:Fat Man U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Man)___ " over the Japanese city of ___E:Nagasaki U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki)___ .

These bombings caused injuries that resulted in the deaths of approximately 200,000 ___E:civilians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian)___ and ___E:military personnel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_personnel)___ .

The ethics of these bombings and their role in ___E:Japan's surrender U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrender_of_Japan)___ are to this day, still ___E:subjects of debate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debate_over_the_atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki)___ .

Since the ___E:atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki)___ , nuclear weapons have been detonated over 2,000 times for ___E:testing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_testing)___ and demonstration.

Only ___E:a few nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons)___ possess such weapons or are suspected of seeking them. The only countries known to have detonated nuclear weapons—and acknowledge possessing them—are (chronologically by date of first test) the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ (succeeded as a nuclear power by ___E:Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ ), the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , ___E:China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , ___E:Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ , and ___E:North Korea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ . ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ is believed to possess nuclear weapons, though, in a ___E:policy of deliberate ambiguity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_of_deliberate_ambiguity)___ , it does not acknowledge having them.   [c] ___E:Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany)___ , ___E:Italy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy)___ , ___E:Turkey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey)___ , ___E:Belgium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium)___ , the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ , and ___E:Belarus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus)___ are ___E:nuclear weapons sharing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing)___ states.  ___E:South Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa)___ is the only country to have ___E:independently developed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ and then ___E:renounced and dismantled U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction#Dismantling)___ its nuclear weapons.

There are two basic types of nuclear weapons: those that derive the majority of their energy from ___E:nuclear fission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission)___ reactions alone, and those that use fission reactions to begin ___E:nuclear fusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion)___ reactions that produce a large amount of the total energy output.
All existing nuclear weapons derive some of their explosive energy from nuclear fission reactions.
Weapons whose explosive output is exclusively from fission reactions are commonly referred to as atomic bombs or atom bombs (abbreviated as A-bombs ).

This has long been noted as something of a ___E:misnomer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misnomer)___ , as their energy comes from the ___E:nucleus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus)___ of the atom, just as it does with fusion weapons.

In fission weapons, a mass of ___E:fissile material U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile_material)___ ( ___E:enriched uranium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_uranium)___ or ___E:plutonium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium)___ ) is forced into ___E:supercriticality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_mass)___ —allowing an ___E:exponential growth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_growth)___ of ___E:nuclear chain reactions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_chain_reaction)___ —either by shooting one piece of sub-critical material into another (the "gun" method) or by compression of a sub-critical sphere or cylinder of fissile material using chemically fueled ___E:explosive lenses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_lens)___ .
The latter approach, the "implosion" method, is more sophisticated and more efficient (smaller, less massive, and requiring less of the expensive fissile fuel) than the former.
A major challenge in all nuclear weapon designs is to ensure that a significant fraction of the fuel is consumed before the weapon destroys itself.

The amount of energy released by fission bombs can range from the equivalent of just under a ton to upwards of 500,000 tons (500 ___E:kilotons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiloton)___ ) of ___E:TNT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT)___ (4.2 to 2.1 × 10 6 GJ).
All fission reactions generate ___E:fission products U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission_product)___ , the remains of the split atomic nuclei.

Many fission products are either highly ___E:radioactive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay)___ (but short-lived) or moderately radioactive (but long-lived), and as such, they are a serious form of ___E:radioactive contamination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_contamination)___ .
Fission products are the principal radioactive component of ___E:nuclear fallout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fallout)___ .
Another source of radioactivity is the burst of free neutrons produced by the weapon.
When they collide with other nuclei in the surrounding material, the neutrons transmute those nuclei into other isotopes, altering their stability and making them radioactive.

The most commonly used fissile materials for nuclear weapons applications have been ___E:uranium-235 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium-235)___ and ___E:plutonium-239 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-239)___ .

Less commonly used has been ___E:uranium-233 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium-233)___ . ___E:Neptunium-237 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptunium-237)___ and some isotopes of ___E:americium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americium)___ may be usable for nuclear explosives as well, but it is not clear that this has ever been implemented, and their plausible use in nuclear weapons is a matter of dispute.
The other basic type of nuclear weapon produces a large proportion of its energy in nuclear fusion reactions.

Such fusion weapons are generally referred to as thermonuclear weapons or more colloquially as hydrogen bombs (abbreviated as H-bombs ), as they rely on fusion reactions between isotopes of ___E:hydrogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen)___ ( ___E:deuterium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium)___ and ___E:tritium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium)___ ).
All such weapons derive a significant portion of their energy from fission reactions used to "trigger" fusion reactions, and fusion reactions can themselves trigger additional fission reactions.

Only six countries—the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ , ___E:Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia)___ , the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ , ___E:China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , and ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India)___ —have conducted thermonuclear weapon tests.

Whether India has detonated a "true" multi-staged ___E:thermonuclear weapon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermonuclear_weapon)___ is controversial.  ___E:North Korea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea)___ claims to have tested a fusion weapon as of January 2016 [update] , though this claim is disputed.
Thermonuclear weapons are considered much more difficult to successfully design and execute than primitive fission weapons.
Almost all of the nuclear weapons deployed today use the thermonuclear design because it results in an explosion hundreds of times stronger than that of a fission bomb of similar weight.

Thermonuclear bombs work by using the energy of a fission bomb to compress and heat fusion fuel. In the ___E:Teller-Ulam design U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teller-Ulam_design)___ , which accounts for all multi-megaton yield hydrogen bombs, this is accomplished by placing a fission bomb and fusion fuel ( ___E:tritium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium)___ , ___E:deuterium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium)___ , or ___E:lithium deuteride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_deuteride)___ ) in proximity within a special, radiation-reflecting container.

When the fission bomb is detonated, ___E:gamma rays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray)___ and ___E:X-rays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray)___ emitted first compress the fusion fuel, then heat it to thermonuclear temperatures.

The ensuing fusion reaction creates enormous numbers of high-speed ___E:neutrons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron)___ , which can then induce fission in materials not normally prone to it, such as ___E:depleted uranium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depleted_uranium)___ .
Each of these components is known as a "stage", with the fission bomb as the "primary" and the fusion capsule as the "secondary".
In large, megaton-range hydrogen bombs, about half of the yield comes from the final fissioning of depleted uranium.

Virtually all thermonuclear weapons deployed today use this "two-stage" design, but it is possible to add additional fusion stages—each stage igniting a larger amount of fusion fuel in the next stage.
This technique can be used to construct thermonuclear weapons of arbitrarily large yield.

This is in contrast to fission bombs, which are limited in their explosive power due to ___E:criticality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_criticality_safety)___ danger (premature nuclear chain reaction caused by too-large amounts of pre-assembled fissile fuel).

The largest nuclear weapon ever detonated, the ___E:Tsar Bomba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba)___ of the USSR, which released an energy equivalent of over 50 megatons of TNT (210 PJ), was a three-stage weapon.
Most thermonuclear weapons are considerably smaller than this, due to practical constraints from missile warhead space and weight requirements.

In the early 1950s the ___E:Livermore Laboratory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Livermore_National_Laboratory)___ in the United States had plans for the testing of two massive bombs, Gnomon and ___E:Sundial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial_(weapon))___ , 1 gigaton of TNT and 10 gigatons of TNT respectively.

Fusion reactions do not create fission products, and thus contribute far less to the creation of ___E:nuclear fallout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fallout)___ than fission reactions, but because all ___E:thermonuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermonuclear_weapon)___ contain at least one ___E:fission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_barrier)___ stage, and many high-yield thermonuclear devices have a final fission stage, thermonuclear weapons can generate at least as much nuclear fallout as fission-only weapons.

Furthermore, high yield thermonuclear explosions (most dangerously ground bursts) have the force to lift radioactive debris upwards past the ___E:tropopause U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropopause)___ into the ___E:stratosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratosphere)___ , where the calm non-turbulent winds permit the debris to travel great distances from the burst, eventually settling and unpredictably contaminating areas far removed from the target of the explosion.

There are other types of nuclear weapons as well. For example, a ___E:boosted fission weapon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boosted_fission_weapon)___ is a fission bomb that increases its explosive yield through a small number of fusion reactions, but it is not a fusion bomb. In the boosted bomb, the neutrons produced by the fusion reactions serve primarily to increase the efficiency of the fission bomb. There are two types of boosted fission bomb: internally boosted, in which a deuterium-tritium mixture is injected into the bomb core, and externally boosted, in which concentric shells of lithium-deuteride and depleted uranium are layered on the outside of the fission bomb core. The external method of boosting enabled the ___E:USSR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR)___ to field the first partially thermonuclear weapons, but it is now obsolete because it demands a spherical bomb geometry, which was adequate during the 1950s arms race when bomber aircraft were the only available delivery vehicles.
The detonation of any nuclear weapon is accompanied by a blast of ___E:neutron radiation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_radiation)___ .

Surrounding a nuclear weapon with suitable materials (such as ___E:cobalt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobalt)___ or ___E:gold U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold)___ ) creates a weapon known as a ___E:salted bomb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salted_bomb)___ .
This device can produce exceptionally large quantities of long-lived ___E:radioactive contamination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_contamination)___ .

It has been conjectured that such a device could serve as a "doomsday weapon" because such a large quantity of radioactivities with half-lives of decades, lifted into the stratosphere where winds would distribute it around the globe, would make all life on the planet extinct.

In connection with the ___E:Strategic Defense Initiative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative)___ , research into the ___E:nuclear pumped laser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_pumped_laser)___ was conducted under the DOD program ___E:Project Excalibur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Excalibur)___ but this did not result in a working weapon.
The concept involves the tapping of the energy of an exploding nuclear bomb to power a single-shot laser that is directed at a distant target.

During the ___E:Starfish Prime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish_Prime)___ high-altitude nuclear test in 1962, an unexpected effect was produced which is called a ___E:nuclear electromagnetic pulse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_electromagnetic_pulse)___ .

This is an intense flash of electromagnetic energy produced by a rain of high-energy electrons which in turn are produced by a nuclear bomb's gamma rays. This flash of energy can permanently destroy or disrupt electronic equipment if insufficiently shielded.
It has been proposed to use this effect to disable an enemy's military and civilian infrastructure as an adjunct to other nuclear or conventional military operations.
By itself it could as well be useful to terrorists for crippling a nation's economic electronics-based infrastructure.

Because the effect is most effectively produced by high altitude nuclear detonations (by military weapons delivered by air, though ground bursts also produce EMP effects over a localized area), it can produce damage to electronics over a wide, even continental, geographical area.

Research has been done into the possibility of ___E:pure fusion bombs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_fusion_weapon)___ : nuclear weapons that consist of fusion reactions without requiring a fission bomb to initiate them. Such a device might provide a simpler path to thermonuclear weapons than one that required the development of fission weapons first, and pure fusion weapons would create significantly less nuclear fallout than other thermonuclear weapons because they would not disperse fission products.

In 1998, the ___E:United States Department of Energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy)___ divulged that the United States had, "...made a substantial investment" in the past to develop pure fusion weapons, but that, "The U.S. does not have and is not developing a pure fusion weapon", and that, "No credible design for a pure fusion weapon resulted from the DOE investment".
___E:Nuclear isomers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_isomers)___ provide a possible pathway to fissionless fusion bombs.

These are naturally occurring ___E:isotopes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes)___ ( ___E:178m2Hf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_hafnium)___ being a prominent example) which exist in an elevated energy state.

Mechanisms to release this energy as bursts of gamma radiation (as in the ___E:hafnium controversy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnium_controversy)___ ) have been proposed as possible triggers for conventional thermonuclear reactions.

___E:Antimatter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter)___ , which consists of ___E:particles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particles)___ resembling ordinary ___E:matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matter)___ particles in most of their properties but having opposite ___E:electric charge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_charge)___ , has been considered as a trigger mechanism for nuclear weapons.
A major obstacle is the difficulty of producing antimatter in large enough quantities, and there is no evidence that it is feasible beyond the military domain.

However, the US Air Force funded studies of the physics of antimatter in the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ , and began considering its possible use in weapons, not just as a trigger, but as the explosive itself.

A fourth generation nuclear weapon design  is related to, and relies upon, the same principle as ___E:antimatter-catalyzed nuclear pulse propulsion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter-catalyzed_nuclear_pulse_propulsion)___ .

Most variation in ___E:nuclear weapon design U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_design)___ is for the purpose of achieving ___E:different yields for different situations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dial-a-yield)___ , and in manipulating design elements to attempt to minimize weapon size,  ___E:radiation hardness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fratricide)___ or requirements for special materials, especially fissile fuel or tritium.

Some nuclear weapons are designed for special purposes; most of these are for non-strategic (decisively war-winning) purposes and are referred to as ___E:tactical nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_nuclear_weapon)___ .

The ___E:neutron bomb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_bomb)___ purportedly conceived by ___E:Sam Cohen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_T._Cohen)___ is a thermonuclear weapon that yields a relatively small explosion but a relatively large amount of neutron ___E:radiation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation)___ .
Such a weapon could, according to tacticians, be used to cause massive biological casualties while leaving inanimate infrastructure mostly intact and creating minimal fallout.

Because high energy neutrons are capable of penetrating dense matter, such as tank armor, neutron warheads were procured in the 1980s (though not deployed in Europe) for use as tactical payloads for US Army artillery shells (200 mm ___E:W79 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W79_Artillery-Fired_Atomic_Projectile)___ and 155 mm ___E:W82 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W82)___ ) and ___E:short range missile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM-52_Lance)___ forces.

Soviet authorities announced similar intentions for neutron warhead deployment in Europe; indeed, they claimed to have originally invented the neutron bomb, but their deployment on USSR tactical nuclear forces is unverifiable. [citation needed]

A type of nuclear explosive most suitable for use by ground special forces was the ___E:Special Atomic Demolition Munition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Atomic_Demolition_Munition)___ , or SADM, sometimes popularly known as a ___E:suitcase nuke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suitcase_nuclear_device)___ .

This is a nuclear bomb that is man-portable, or at least truck-portable, and though of a relatively small yield (one or two kilotons) is sufficient to destroy important tactical targets such as bridges, dams, tunnels, important military or commercial installations, etc. either behind enemy lines or pre-emptively on friendly territory soon to be overtaken by invading enemy forces.
These weapons require plutonium fuel and are particularly "dirty".
They also demand especially stringent security precautions in their storage and deployment. [citation needed]
Small "tactical" nuclear weapons were deployed for use as antiaircraft weapons.

Examples include the USAF ___E:AIR-2 Genie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIR-2_Genie)___ , the ___E:AIM-26 Falcon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIM-26_Falcon)___ and US Army ___E:Nike Hercules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike_Hercules)___ .

The system used to ___E:deliver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_delivery)___ a nuclear weapon to its target is an important factor affecting both ___E:nuclear weapon design U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_design)___ and ___E:nuclear strategy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warfare)___ .

The design, development, and maintenance of delivery systems are among the most expensive parts of a nuclear weapons program; they account, for example, for 57% of the financial resources spent by the United States on nuclear weapons projects since 1940.

The simplest method for delivering a nuclear weapon is a ___E:gravity bomb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_bomb)___ dropped from ___E:aircraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft)___ ; this was the method used by the ___E:United States against Japan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki)___ in 1945. This method places few restrictions on the size of the weapon.

It does, however, limit attack range, response time to an impending attack, and the number of weapons that a country can field at the same time. With miniaturization, nuclear bombs can be delivered by both ___E:strategic bombers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bomber)___ and tactical ___E:fighter-bombers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter-bomber)___ .

This method is the primary means of nuclear weapons delivery; the majority of US nuclear warheads, for example, are free-fall gravity bombs, namely the ___E:B61 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B61_nuclear_bomb)___ , which is being improved upon to this day.

Preferable from a strategic point of view is a nuclear weapon mounted on a ___E:missile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile)___ , which can use a ___E:ballistic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistics)___ trajectory to deliver the warhead over the horizon.

Although even short-range missiles allow for a faster and less vulnerable attack, the development of long-range ___E:intercontinental ballistic missiles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile)___ (ICBMs) and ___E:submarine-launched ballistic missiles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine-launched_ballistic_missile)___ (SLBMs) has given some nations the ability to plausibly deliver missiles anywhere on the globe with a high likelihood of success.

More advanced systems, such as ___E:multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_independently_targetable_reentry_vehicle)___ (MIRVs), can launch multiple warheads at different targets from one missile, reducing the chance of a successful ___E:missile defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_defense)___ .
Today, missiles are most common among systems designed for delivery of nuclear weapons.
Making a warhead small enough to fit onto a missile, though, can be difficult.

___E:Tactical weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_nuclear_weapon)___ have involved the most variety of delivery types, including not only gravity bombs and missiles but also ___E:artillery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_artillery)___ shells, ___E:land mines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_demolition_munition)___ , and ___E:nuclear depth charges U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_depth_charge)___ and ___E:torpedoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_torpedo)___ for ___E:anti-submarine warfare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-submarine_warfare)___ .
An atomic ___E:mortar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(weapon))___ has been tested by the United States.

Small, two-man portable tactical weapons (somewhat misleadingly referred to as ___E:suitcase bombs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suitcase_bomb)___ ), such as the ___E:Special Atomic Demolition Munition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Atomic_Demolition_Munition)___ , have been developed, although the difficulty of combining sufficient yield with portability limits their military utility.

Nuclear warfare strategy is a set of policies that deal with preventing or fighting a nuclear war. The policy of trying to prevent an attack by a nuclear weapon from another country by threatening nuclear retaliation is known as the strategy of ___E:nuclear deterrence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterrence_theory)___ .

The goal in deterrence is to always maintain a second strike capability (the ability of a country to respond to a nuclear attack with one of its own) and potentially to strive for ___E:first strike U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-emptive_nuclear_strike)___ status (the ability to destroy an enemy's nuclear forces before they could retaliate).

During the Cold War, policy and military theorists considered the sorts of policies that might prevent a nuclear attack, and they developed ___E:game theory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_theory)___ models that could lead to stable deterrence conditions.
Different forms of ___E:nuclear weapons delivery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_delivery)___ (see above) allow for different types of nuclear strategies.

The goals of any strategy are generally to make it difficult for an enemy to launch a pre-emptive strike against the weapon system and difficult to defend against the delivery of the weapon during a potential conflict.

This can mean keeping weapon locations hidden, such as deploying them on ___E:submarines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine)___ or land mobile ___E:transporter erector launchers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transporter_erector_launcher)___ whose locations are difficult to track, or it can mean protecting weapons by burying them in hardened ___E:missile silo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_silo)___ bunkers.

Other components of nuclear strategies included using missile defenses to destroy the missiles before they land or implementing ___E:civil defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_defense)___ measures using early-warning systems to evacuate citizens to safe areas before an attack.
Weapons designed to threaten large populations or to deter attacks are known as strategic weapons.
Nuclear weapons for use on a ___E:battlefield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle)___ in military situations are called tactical weapons.
Critics of nuclear war strategy often suggest that a nuclear war between two nations would result in mutual annihilation.

From this point of view, the significance of nuclear weapons is to deter war because any nuclear war would escalate out of mutual distrust and fear, resulting in ___E:mutually assured destruction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction)___ .
This threat of national, if not global, destruction has been a strong motivation for anti-nuclear weapons activism.
Critics from the peace movement and within the military establishment [citation needed] have questioned the usefulness of such weapons in the current military climate.

According to an ___E:advisory opinion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice_advisory_opinion_on_the_Legality_of_the_Threat_or_Use_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ issued by the ___E:International Court of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice)___ in 1996, the use of (or threat of use of) such weapons would generally be contrary to the rules of international law applicable in armed conflict, but the court did not reach an opinion as to whether or not the threat or use would be lawful in specific extreme circumstances such as if the survival of the state were at stake.
Another ___E:deterrence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterrence_theory)___ position is that ___E:nuclear proliferation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_proliferation)___ can be desirable.

In this case, it is argued that, unlike conventional weapons, nuclear weapons deter all-out war between states, and they succeeded in doing this during the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ between the US and the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ .

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Gen. ___E:Pierre Marie Gallois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Marie_Gallois)___ of France, an adviser to ___E:Charles de Gaulle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle)___ , argued in books like The Balance of Terror: Strategy for the Nuclear Age (1961) that mere possession of a nuclear arsenal was enough to ensure deterrence, and thus concluded that the spread of nuclear weapons could increase ___E:international stability U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_peace)___ .

Some prominent ___E:neo-realist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neorealism_(international_relations))___ scholars, such as ___E:Kenneth Waltz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Waltz)___ and ___E:John Mearsheimer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mearsheimer)___ , have argued, along the lines of Gallois, that some forms of nuclear proliferation would decrease the likelihood of ___E:total war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_war)___ , especially in troubled regions of the world where there exists a single nuclear-weapon state.

Aside from the public opinion that opposes proliferation in any form, there are two schools of thought on the matter: those, like Mearsheimer, who favored selective proliferation,  and Waltz, who was somewhat more non- ___E:interventionist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interventionism_(politics))___ .

Interest in proliferation and the ___E:stability-instability paradox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability-instability_paradox)___ that it generates continues to this day, with ongoing debate about indigenous Japanese and ___E:South Korean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea)___ nuclear deterrent against ___E:North Korea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea)___ .
The threat of potentially suicidal terrorists possessing nuclear weapons (a form of ___E:nuclear terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_terrorism)___ ) complicates the decision process.
The prospect of ___E:mutually assured destruction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction)___ might not deter an enemy who expects to die in the confrontation.

Further, if the initial act is from a stateless ___E:terrorist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist)___ instead of a sovereign nation, there might not be a nation or specific target to retaliate against.

It has been argued, especially after the ___E:September 11, 2001, attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ , that this complication calls for a new nuclear strategy, one that is distinct from that which gave relative stability during the Cold War.  Since 1996, the United States has had a policy of allowing the targeting of its nuclear weapons at terrorists armed with ___E:weapons of mass destruction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapons_of_mass_destruction)___ .

___E:Robert Gallucci U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gallucci)___ argues that although traditional deterrence is not an effective approach toward terrorist groups bent on causing a nuclear catastrophe, Gallucci believes that "the United States should instead consider a policy of expanded deterrence, which focuses not solely on the would-be nuclear terrorists but on those states that may deliberately transfer or inadvertently leak nuclear weapons and materials to them. By threatening retaliation against those states, the United States may be able to deter that which it cannot physically prevent."

___E:Graham Allison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Allison)___ makes a similar case, arguing that the key to expanded deterrence is coming up with ways of tracing nuclear material to the country that forged the fissile material. "After a nuclear bomb detonates, ___E:nuclear forensics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_forensics)___ cops would collect debris samples and send them to a laboratory for radiological analysis.

By identifying unique attributes of the fissile material, including its impurities and contaminants, one could trace the path back to its origin." The process is analogous to identifying a criminal by fingerprints. "The goal would be twofold: first, to deter leaders of nuclear states from selling weapons to terrorists by holding them accountable for any use of their weapons; second, to give leaders every incentive to tightly secure their nuclear weapons and materials."

According to the Pentagon's June 2019 " ___E:Doctrine for Joint Nuclear Operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine_for_Joint_Nuclear_Operations)___ " of the Joint Chiefs of Staffs website Publication, "Integration of nuclear weapons employment with conventional and special operations forces is essential to the success of any mission or operation."
Because they are weapons of mass destruction, the proliferation and possible use of nuclear weapons are important issues in international relations and diplomacy.

In most countries, the use of nuclear force can only be authorized by the ___E:head of government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government)___ or ___E:head of state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state)___ . The ___E:Russell–Einstein Manifesto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell%E2%80%93Einstein_Manifesto)___ was issued in ___E:London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)___ on July 9, 1955, by ___E:Bertrand Russell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_Russell)___ in the midst of the Cold War. It highlighted the dangers posed by nuclear weapons and called for world leaders to seek peaceful resolutions to international conflict.

The signatories included eleven pre-eminent intellectuals and scientists, including ___E:Albert Einstein U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein)___ , who signed it just days before his death on April 18, 1955. A few days after the release, philanthropist ___E:Cyrus S. Eaton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_S._Eaton)___ offered to sponsor a conference—called for in the manifesto—in ___E:Pugwash, Nova Scotia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pugwash,_Nova_Scotia)___ , Eaton's birthplace.

This conference was to be the first of the ___E:Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pugwash_Conferences_on_Science_and_World_Affairs)___ , held in July 1957.

By the 1960s, steps were taken to limit both the proliferation of nuclear weapons to other countries and the environmental effects of ___E:nuclear testing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_testing)___ .

The ___E:Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty)___ (1963) restricted all nuclear testing to ___E:underground nuclear testing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_nuclear_testing)___ , to prevent contamination from nuclear fallout, whereas the ___E:Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ (1968) attempted to place restrictions on the types of activities signatories could participate in, with the goal of allowing the transference of non-military ___E:nuclear technology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_technology)___ to member countries without fear of proliferation.

In 1957, the ___E:International Atomic Energy Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency)___ (IAEA) was established under the mandate of the ___E:United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations)___ to encourage development of peaceful applications of nuclear technology, provide international safeguards against its misuse, and facilitate the application of safety measures in its use. A testing ban imposes a significant hindrance to nuclear arms development by any complying country.
The Treaty requires the ratification by 44 specific states before it can go into force; as of 2012 [update] , the ratification of eight of these states is still required.

Additional treaties and agreements have governed nuclear weapons stockpiles between the countries with the two largest stockpiles, the United States and the Soviet Union, and later between the United States and Russia.

These include treaties such as ___E:SALT II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SALT_II)___ (never ratified), ___E:START I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_I)___ (expired), ___E:INF U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate-Range_Nuclear_Forces_Treaty)___ , ___E:START II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_II)___ (never in effect), ___E:SORT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SORT)___ , and ___E:New START U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START)___ , as well as non-binding agreements such as ___E:SALT I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SALT_I)___ and the Presidential Nuclear Initiatives  of 1991. Even when they did not enter into force, these agreements helped limit and later reduce the numbers and types of nuclear weapons between the United States and the Soviet Union/Russia.
Nuclear weapons have also been opposed by agreements between countries.

Many nations have been declared ___E:Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-Weapon-Free_Zone)___ , areas where nuclear weapons production and deployment are prohibited, through the use of treaties.

The ___E:Treaty of Tlatelolco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tlatelolco)___ (1967) prohibited any production or deployment of nuclear weapons in ___E:Latin America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America)___ and the ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ , and the ___E:Treaty of Pelindaba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Pelindaba)___ (1964) prohibits nuclear weapons in many African countries.

As recently as 2006 a ___E:Central Asian Nuclear Weapon Free Zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asian_Nuclear_Weapon_Free_Zone)___ was established among the former Soviet republics of Central Asia prohibiting nuclear weapons.

In 1996, the ___E:International Court of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice)___ , the highest court of the United Nations, issued an Advisory Opinion concerned with the " ___E:Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice_advisory_opinion_on_the_Legality_of_the_Threat_or_Use_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ ".

The court ruled that the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons would violate various articles of ___E:international law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law)___ , including the ___E:Geneva Conventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Conventions)___ , the ___E:Hague Conventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hague_Conventions_(1899_and_1907))___ , the ___E:UN Charter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Charter)___ , and the ___E:Universal Declaration of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights)___ .

Given the unique, destructive characteristics of nuclear weapons, the ___E:International Committee of the Red Cross U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross)___ calls on States to ensure that these weapons are never used, irrespective of whether they consider them lawful or not.

Additionally, there have been other, specific actions meant to discourage countries from developing nuclear arms. One of the stated casus belli for the initiation of the 2003 ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ was an accusation by the United States that Iraq was actively pursuing nuclear arms (though this was soon discovered ___E:not to be the case U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger_uranium_forgeries)___ as the program had been discontinued).

In 1981, Israel had ___E:bombed a nuclear reactor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Opera)___ being constructed in ___E:Osirak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osirak)___ , ___E:Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq)___ , in what it called an attempt to halt Iraq's previous nuclear arms ambitions; in 2007, Israel ___E:bombed another reactor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Orchard)___ being constructed in ___E:Syria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria)___ .

In 2013, ___E:Mark Diesendorf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Diesendorf)___ said that governments of France, India, North Korea, Pakistan, UK, and South Africa have used nuclear power or research reactors to assist nuclear weapons development or to contribute to their supplies of nuclear explosives from military reactors.

In 2017, 122 countries mainly in the ___E:Global South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_South)___ voted in favor of adopting the ___E:Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons)___ , which eventually entered into force in 2021.

The ___E:Doomsday Clock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_Clock)___ measures the likelihood of a human-made ___E:global catastrophe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_catastrophic_risk)___ and is published annually by the ___E:Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulletin_of_the_Atomic_Scientists)___ .

In 2023, following the ___E:escalation of nuclear threats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_threats_during_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ during the ___E:Russian invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ , the doomsday clock was set to 90 seconds, the highest likelihood of global catastrophe since the existence of the Doomsday Clock.

As of 2024, Russia has intensified nuclear threats in Ukraine and is reportedly planning to place nuclear weapons in orbit, breaching the ___E:1967 Outer Space Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Space_Treaty)___ .

Nuclear disarmament refers to both the act of reducing or eliminating nuclear weapons and to the end state of a nuclear-free world, in which nuclear weapons are eliminated.

Critics of nuclear disarmament say that it would undermine the present ___E:nuclear peace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_peace)___ and deterrence and would lead to increased global instability.

Some analysts have argued that nuclear weapons have made the world relatively safer, with peace through ___E:deterrence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterrence_theory)___ and through the ___E:stability–instability paradox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability%E2%80%93instability_paradox)___ , including in south Asia.   ___E:Kenneth Waltz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Waltz)___ has argued that nuclear weapons have helped keep an uneasy peace, and further nuclear weapon proliferation might even help avoid the large scale conventional wars that were so common before their invention at the end of ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

But former Secretary ___E:Henry Kissinger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger)___ said in 2010 that there is a new danger, which cannot be addressed by deterrence: "The classical notion of deterrence was that there was some consequences before which aggressors and evildoers would recoil.
